meta.name: Razor Mini — Rapid Reasoning Drill Set
meta.notes: Tu quoque / hypocrisy items are filed under ad_hominem for this build. 'valid' items are deliberately designed to resemble one of the three fallacies so players cannot pass on vibes alone.

items.prompt:
Person A: "The data shows the new traffic scheme cut accidents by 20% in its first year."
Person B: "You've never even owned a car. Why would anyone listen to you about roads?"
items.explanation: B never touches the accident data. Whether A drives is irrelevant to whether the statistic is accurate — the attack targets A's standing, not A's claim.

items.prompt: Of course she thinks the wealth tax is a good idea — she's a trust fund kid who's never worked a day in her life.
items.explanation: Her background is offered as a substitute for engaging with the argument. Even if the biography is accurate, it tells you nothing about whether the tax policy works.

items.prompt:
Person A: "I've read the report and I think the budget forecast is too optimistic."
Person B: "Mate, you failed A-level maths. Sit down."
items.explanation: A past exam result is used to disqualify A from speaking. The forecast is either too optimistic or it isn't — that's settled by checking the numbers, not A's transcript.

items.prompt:
Person A: "You really shouldn't drive after two pints."
Person B: "You drove home from Jake's party last summer. Don't lecture me."
items.explanation: Tu quoque — the 'you too' variant. A's own past behaviour might make A a hypocrite, but it does nothing to make drink-driving safe.

items.prompt: This nutrition advice comes from a guy who's visibly overweight, so it's obviously nonsense.
items.explanation: The speaker's body is treated as a refutation. Advice can be sound whether or not the person giving it follows it — the evidence behind the advice is the only thing that settles it.

items.prompt:
Person A: "The council's housing plan won't hit its targets — here's the shortfall in the numbers."
Person B: "Funny how you only started caring about housing once you decided to run for office."
items.explanation: Circumstantial ad hominem: B attacks A's motive rather than the shortfall. A self-interested person can still be pointing at a real gap in the plan.

items.prompt: My doctor told me to quit smoking, but I saw her smoking outside the clinic — so clearly it can't be that dangerous.
items.explanation: Tu quoque. The doctor's inconsistency is real, but the health risk of smoking is established by the research, not by whether she personally complies with it.

items.prompt: You can't trust a word he says about climate policy — the man's been divorced twice and can't even keep his own life together.
items.explanation: Personal life is dragged in as though it bears on policy analysis. There's no route from marital history to the merits of a carbon pricing argument.

items.prompt: The lead author of that study is a vegan, so obviously the findings on red meat are rubbish.
items.explanation: The author's diet is used to bin the result outright. Noting a possible bias is fair as a reason to check the methodology — using it as the whole rebuttal is the fallacy.

items.prompt: Environmentalists lecture us about flying less and then jet off to conferences — so the whole climate thing is clearly overblown.
items.explanation: Tu quoque aimed at a group. Inconsistent advocates are a fair target for criticism, but atmospheric physics doesn't depend on their travel habits.

items.prompt:
Person A: "I think we could trim the defence budget by a couple of percent."
Person B: "So you'd rather we had no army at all and just hoped nobody invaded?"
items.explanation: A modest trim is inflated into total abolition, and B then attacks the inflated version. The position actually on the table was never addressed.

items.prompt: The people asking for bike lanes basically want to make driving illegal.
items.explanation: A request to accommodate cyclists is restated as prohibiting drivers. The distortion turns a shared-space argument into an attack on car owners.

items.prompt:
Person A: "I don't think this candidate is our strongest option."
Person B: "So you're happy for the other lot to win. Great. Thanks a lot."
items.explanation: Criticism of one candidate is recast as support for the opposition. A's actual view — that a better option exists — vanishes from the exchange.

items.prompt:
Person A: "I'd like us to do a bit more code review before merging to main."
Person B: "Right, so you want to slow the whole team to a crawl and ship absolutely nothing."
items.explanation: 'More review' becomes 'ship nothing', an absurd endpoint nobody proposed. Attacking that endpoint leaves the real suggestion untouched.

items.prompt: Anyone who supports remote work is really just saying they don't want to work at all.
items.explanation: A claim about where work happens is reframed as a claim about whether work happens. The substitute position is trivially easy to dismiss.

items.prompt:
Person A: "I think the tipping system is unfair to servers."
Person B: "So you think servers should just work for free, then?"
items.explanation: B inverts the position entirely — A's complaint is that servers are underpaid, and B attacks a view that would pay them nothing.

items.prompt:
Person A: "Consent should be part of the secondary school curriculum."
Person B: "You want to expose children to explicit sexual content in a classroom."
items.explanation: The proposal is relabelled with the most lurid framing available. B fights that framing rather than the age-appropriate curriculum A described.

items.prompt: So because I forgot one anniversary, apparently I'm a terrible partner who has never done a single thing for you.
items.explanation: A specific complaint is escalated into a sweeping condemnation, which is then rejected as unfair. The original grievance never gets answered.

items.prompt:
Person A: "Vaccine side effects should be monitored and reported transparently."
Person B: "So you're an anti-vaxxer."
items.explanation: A mainstream position on pharmacovigilance is swapped for a fringe label. The label is easier to attack than the actual point about transparency.

items.prompt: People calling for police reform are saying they want zero consequences for anyone who commits a crime.
items.explanation: 'Reform' is redefined as 'no consequences' — a position almost nobody holds. The redefinition does the argumentative work that evidence should be doing.

items.prompt: You're either with us on this restructure, or you're against the company's future. Simple as that.
items.explanation: Two options are presented as the only ones available. Supporting the company while opposing this particular restructure is an obvious third position the framing hides.

items.prompt:
Person A: "I've got some concerns about the merger timeline."
Person B: "So do you want the merger or not? Yes or no."
items.explanation: A nuanced position is forced into a binary that can't contain it. 'Yes, but later' and 'yes, with conditions' are both ruled out by the framing rather than by argument.

items.prompt: We can have a strong economy or a clean environment. There is no third road.
items.explanation: The two goals are asserted to be mutually exclusive with no middle ground. Policies that trade off partially, or serve both, are excluded by assertion alone.

items.prompt:
Person A: "I'd rather skip the party tonight, I'm exhausted."
Person B: "Fine. So either you come out tonight, or you admit you don't actually care about this friendship."
items.explanation: Attendance and affection are welded into a single binary. Being tired and being a good friend are entirely compatible — the dilemma is manufactured for leverage.

items.prompt:
Person A: "The council has to choose: fund the new library, or repair the roads."
Person B: "The library, I suppose."
items.explanation: A budget with many possible allocations is presented as a straight choice between two items. Partial funding, phasing, or other savings are never put on the table.

items.prompt: Either you go to university, or you throw your future away.
items.explanation: Apprenticeships, trades, employment and starting later are all erased. The choice looks forced only because the alternatives were left out.

items.prompt:
Person A: "I don't think banning the app outright is the right move."
Person B: "So you'd let a hostile government harvest every citizen's data? Choose."
items.explanation: The options are reduced to total ban or total inaction. Data localisation, audits and disclosure rules sit between them and are silently dropped.

items.prompt:
Person A: "This module needs refactoring before we pile more features on it."
Person B: "We can refactor or we can hit the deadline. Which is it?"
items.explanation: The framing assumes refactoring is all-or-nothing. Partial cleanup, cutting scope, or refactoring the one hot path are all available and unmentioned.

items.prompt: You either accept the science completely or you're a denier.
items.explanation: Scientific findings vary in how well established they are, and questioning one result is not rejecting a field. The binary leaves no room for calibrated confidence.

items.prompt: We can protect free speech, or we can moderate harmful content. Choose one.
items.explanation: There is a real tension here, but presenting it as a strict either/or is still the fallacy. Narrow, transparent, appealable moderation rules are a live third option the framing forecloses.

items.prompt:
Person A: "Trust me, this supplement is clinically proven to work."
Person B: "You're paid by the company that makes it and you haven't shown me the trial. That's a reason for me to want independent evidence before I accept it."
items.explanation: Looks like ad hominem, but isn't. B doesn't conclude the supplement fails — B identifies a real reason A's testimony is unreliable and asks for evidence instead. Questioning a source's credibility is legitimate when the claim rests on that source's word.

items.prompt:
Person A: "Nobody should need a licence to own any weapon at all."
Person B: "So your position is no licensing whatsoever, including automatic weapons?"
Person A: "Correct."
items.explanation: Looks like a strawman, but isn't. B restates the position in its strongest and most literal form and checks it — and A confirms. Accurately describing an extreme view that someone actually holds is not distortion.

items.prompt: The bill either passes tonight's vote or it doesn't. There's no third outcome on the order paper.
items.explanation: Looks like a false dilemma, but the binary is genuinely exhaustive. A dilemma is only a fallacy when real options have been left out; here the two branches cover every possibility.

items.prompt:
Person A: "I'm not convinced this bridge design is safe."
Person B: "What's your reasoning? The load calculations are in section four — which figure do you think is wrong?"
items.explanation: B could have gone after A's credentials and instead goes after the argument, asking for the specific point of disagreement. This is what engaging with a claim looks like rather than dismissing the person making it.

items.prompt: Three separate studies using different methods found the same effect, and none has found the opposite. That's decent — though not conclusive — reason to think the effect is real.
items.explanation: The strength of the conclusion is matched to the strength of the evidence. Independent replication supports the claim, and the hedge is stated rather than glossed over.

items.prompt: We have one engineer and two weeks, so we can ship payments or notifications this sprint, not both. Either one could go into next sprint instead.
items.explanation: Looks like a false dilemma, but it's a real constraint honestly stated — and it explicitly leaves the third option open. The exclusivity comes from the actual resource limit, not from the framing.

items.prompt:
Person A: "Immigration has no effect on wages whatsoever."
Person B: "That's a strong claim. The literature is mixed, with small negative effects in some low-wage sectors. Which studies are you relying on?"
items.explanation: B challenges an absolute claim by citing the state of the evidence and asking for A's basis. The position isn't exaggerated and A isn't attacked — the claim itself is put under pressure.

items.prompt: You said the shop is closed on Sundays, but I bought bread there last Sunday afternoon. So it isn't.
items.explanation: A universal claim is refuted by a single clear counterexample. The reasoning goes straight at the content of the claim and one instance is logically enough to sink it.

items.prompt: If the server had gone down, the monitoring alerts would have fired. No alerts fired. So the server didn't go down.
items.explanation: Valid conditional reasoning — deny the consequent, deny the antecedent. It depends on the monitoring being reliable, but that premise is stated rather than hidden.

items.prompt:
Person A: "Your cost estimate left out ongoing maintenance."
Person B: "You're right, it did. Adding maintenance takes the total to £1.2m, which changes my conclusion."
items.explanation: A specific, relevant objection is met by checking it and updating. No distortion, no counterattack, no forced binary — this is what the honest version of the exchange looks like.
